result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B explains why both extremes fail: keystroke checks flag half-typed input, and submit-only checks leave errors such as a taken username until the end. It then recommends checking on blur, with errors shown only after a field has been touched and cleared live once fixed. A advises against checking on blur and gives a weak account of why submit-only fails, though its handling of each field (debounced username check, password checklist, errors that clear live) is strong. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer A meets every rubric item. It explains why both extremes fail, recommends checking a field when the person leaves it, and says not to show errors on fields they haven't touched. Once an error shows, it re-checks as they type, and it gives specific handling for each of the three fields. Answer B has strong field-specific detail and accessibility advice, but it argues against checking on leaving a field and keeps submit as the main trigger, which goes against item 2. It also never names the main weakness of submit-only checking, which is a pile of errors at the end.
